sections.title: A goddess made of river mud
sections.intro_md:
Every year, from about June, a narrow lane of workshops in north Kolkata called **Kumartuli** fills with straw skeletons. Men wrap bamboo frames in straw, then slap on clay dug from the bed of the **Hooghly**, the branch of the Ganga that runs past the door. By late September the frames have become ten-armed goddesses with huge eyes, standing on lions, spearing a buffalo demon.

For five days in autumn, Kolkata turns into an open-air museum of several thousand of these images, in pandals built to look like temples, ships, palaces or protest art. On the last day, the same clay goddesses are carried back to the river and sunk. The mud goes home.

In **December 2021** UNESCO added **Durga Puja in Kolkata** to its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. A British Council study put the festival's creative economy at about **₹32,377 crore** in 2019, roughly 2.6% of the state's GDP.

That is West Bengal in one scene: devout, secular and artistic at once, spending a fortune on something it will sink in the river.

spotlights.name: Kumartuli, the potters' quarter
spotlights.when: Potters settled here from the early 18th century
spotlights.spot_it: A lane of open-fronted sheds full of half-finished clay goddesses, straw showing through, faces painted last.
spotlights.story_md: About **450 to 550 workshops** crowd Kumartuli, run by families of *kumors* (potters) who came from Krishnanagar and elsewhere in rural Bengal. The image is built in layers: a bamboo frame, tied straw, a coarse clay mixed with rice husk, then fine river silt. Tradition asks that a pinch of soil be collected from the doorstep of a sex worker's house, the *punya mati*, a gesture often read as saying that nobody is excluded from the goddess. The eyes are painted last, on a day called *chokkhu daan*, the gift of eyes. Kumartuli images now ship by sea to Durga Pujas in London, Sydney and Toronto.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Nearly every big Durga image in Bengal starts in this lane.
spotlights.memory_hook: Straw bones, river skin, painted eyes last.

spotlights.name: Durga Puja in Kolkata
spotlights.when: Five main days in Ashvin (September to October); UNESCO list 2021
spotlights.spot_it: A ten-armed goddess on a lion, flanked by Lakshmi, Saraswati, Ganesha and Kartik, all on one frame under a single arched backdrop.
spotlights.story_md: Bengal's Durga is a daughter coming home to her parents for five days with her four children, not only a warrior. The big household pujas of the 1700s, such as **Sovabazar Rajbari** where Robert Clive is said to have attended in 1757, gave way to the *sarbojanin*, or community, puja after **1910**, funded by neighbourhood clubs. Today the city has more than **3,000** community pujas. On **Dashami**, the last day, married women smear vermilion on the goddess and on each other in *sindoor khela*, and the images are taken to the river.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the biggest public art event in India and the anchor of the Bengali year.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five days, three thousand goddesses, one river.

sections.title: The state at a glance
sections.intro_md:
West Bengal is the **only Indian state that runs from the Himalaya to the sea**. It covers **88,752 km²**, about the size of Portugal, and is long and thin: roughly 600 km from the Kanchenjunga ridge in the north to the Bay of Bengal in the south, and only about 20 km wide at the **Siliguri Corridor**, the 'chicken's neck' that joins the northeast to the rest of India.

It had **91.3 million** people in 2011, the fourth most of any state, and an estimated 100 million now. Its density, **1,028 per km²** in 2011, was second only to Bihar. It shares about **2,217 km** of border with Bangladesh, the longest of any state, plus borders with Nepal and Bhutan and five Indian states.

It was carved out of British Bengal on **15 August 1947**, when the Muslim-majority east went to Pakistan and later became Bangladesh. It has **23 districts**, **294** assembly seats and **42** Lok Sabha seats, and its economy, about **₹17 lakh crore** in 2023 to 24, is India's sixth largest.

spotlights.name: Kolkata
spotlights.when: Capital of British India 1772 to 1911; renamed from Calcutta in 2001
spotlights.spot_it: Yellow taxis, crumbling colonnaded mansions, a huge green Maidan, and a river crossed by a steel cantilever bridge.
spotlights.story_md: Kolkata grew from three villages, **Sutanuti, Gobindapur and Kalikata**, that the East India Company bought in **1698**. It was the capital of British India until **1911** and, for much of the 1800s, the second city of the British Empire after London. The official name changed from Calcutta to Kolkata on **1 January 2001**. Today the metro area holds about **15 million** people. It built **India's first metro** (1984), hosts India's oldest museum (1814), and is the only Indian city where trams still run, if barely.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was the place where modern India's politics, science, art and business took shape.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three villages bought for about 1,300 rupees became the Empire's second city.

spotlights.name: Howrah Bridge (Rabindra Setu)
spotlights.spot_it: A grey steel cantilever with two tall towers and no piers in the water, carrying a river of buses, carts and porters.
spotlights.story_md: The bridge has **no pillars in the river**: two towers on the banks hold arms that meet in the middle, a 457 m main span. It was built during the Second World War, using about **26,500 tonnes** of steel, most of it from Tata Steel, and held together with **rivets, not nuts and bolts**. It opened quietly in **1943** because of fears of Japanese bombing. About **100,000 vehicles** and even more pedestrians cross daily. In 1965 it was renamed **Rabindra Setu** after Tagore, though almost nobody calls it that. Its biggest enemy is human: spit. Chewed tobacco ate into the steel hoods of the pillars, which had to be armoured with fibreglass.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most used cantilever bridge in the world and Kolkata's logo.
spotlights.memory_hook: A war-time bridge with no bolts, no river pillars, and a spit problem.

sections.title: From Kanchenjunga to the mangroves
sections.intro_md:
Travel north to south and you cross four countries' worth of landscape. At the top are the **Darjeeling and Kalimpong hills**, tea and Buddhist monasteries on ridges facing Kanchenjunga, the world's third highest peak. Below them lie the **Dooars and Terai**, forest and grassland where one-horned rhinos and elephants live at Jaldapara and Gorumara.

Then comes the vast flat **Gangetic delta**, some of the most fertile and crowded farmland on Earth, crossed by the Ganga and its branches. At **Farakka**, a barrage built in 1975 pushes part of the Ganga's water into the **Hooghly** to keep Kolkata's port from silting up, a sore point with Bangladesh ever since. The main Ganga flows on east into Bangladesh as the **Padma**.

At the bottom is the **Sundarbans**, a maze of tidal rivers, mud and mangrove shared with Bangladesh, home to the only tigers in the world that live in a mangrove forest.

The state animal is the **fishing cat**; the state fish, inevitably, the **ilish**.

spotlights.name: Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny blue steam engine pulling two toy-sized coaches along a road, almost brushing the shopfronts.
spotlights.story_md: The 'toy train' climbs about **2,000 m in 88 km** on a track only **2 feet (610 mm)** wide. With no room for tunnels or wide curves, the engineers used **loops**, where the line spirals over itself, and **zig-zag reverses**, where the train backs up a slope and then goes forward again. At **Batasia Loop** the train circles a war memorial with Kanchenjunga behind it. **Ghum**, at about 2,258 m, was long the highest railway station in India. In **1999** it became only the second railway in the world on UNESCO's list.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how Victorian engineers climbed a Himalayan ridge on a shoestring gauge.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two feet of track, two kilometres of climb, one loop round a war memorial.

spotlights.name: Sandakphu and the Sleeping Buddha
spotlights.when: Highest point of the state, 3,636 m
spotlights.spot_it: A bare ridge with a few lodges, and on the horizon a wall of snow peaks shaped like a reclining figure.
spotlights.story_md: Sandakphu sits right on the **India to Nepal border**; the trail weaves in and out of Nepal. From the top on a clear morning you can see **four of the world's five highest mountains**: Everest, Lhotse, Makalu and Kanchenjunga. The Kanchenjunga massif seen from here looks like a person lying down, nicknamed the **Sleeping Buddha**. The ridge is part of **Singalila National Park**, home to red pandas.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives a lowland, sea-level state a 3,636 m summit with a view of Everest.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four of the five highest peaks from one Bengali hilltop.

spotlights.name: The Sundarbans
spotlights.spot_it: Low green walls of mangrove along brown tidal channels, with spiky breathing roots poking out of the mud at low tide.
spotlights.story_md: The Sundarbans is the **largest mangrove forest in the world**, about 10,000 km², of which roughly **40% lies in India**. Mangrove trees such as the *sundari*, which may give the forest its name, push up **pneumatophores**, pencil-like roots that breathe air. Around **4.5 million people** live in the Indian Sundarbans on islands protected by earth embankments. Cyclones Aila (2009), Amphan (2020) and Yaas (2021) broke those walls and salted the fields. Islands such as **Ghoramara** have lost more than half their land to the sea since the 1970s.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shields Kolkata from cyclones and is one of the frontlines of rising seas.
spotlights.memory_hook: A forest that floods twice a day and breathes through its roots.

spotlights.name: The Sundarbans tiger
spotlights.when: About 100 tigers counted in the Indian part (2022)
spotlights.spot_it: A tiger swimming across a wide brown creek, or pug marks in grey mud at the water's edge.
spotlights.story_md: These tigers **swim between islands**, drink brackish water and eat fish, crabs and monitor lizards as well as deer and wild boar. The 2022 national count found about **100** in the Indian Sundarbans. They are also notorious for attacking people: honey collectors, woodcutters and crab fishers are killed every year, leaving villages of so-called *tiger widows*. In the 1980s forest officers handed out **face masks to be worn on the back of the head**, because tigers usually attack from behind; for a while attacks on mask wearers dropped.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They are the only tigers adapted to a tidal mangrove, and among the hardest to count.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tiger that swims, eats crabs and was fooled by a mask on the back of a head.

spotlights.name: Fishing cat, the state animal
spotlights.spot_it: A stocky, spotted cat twice the size of a house cat, with short legs, a short tail and slightly webbed front paws.
spotlights.story_md: The fishing cat lives in the marshes, reed beds and mangroves of the delta, including the **East Kolkata Wetlands** at the city's edge. It hunts by tapping the water's surface to mimic insects, then **scooping fish out with its paw** or diving in head first. It is listed as Vulnerable, because wetlands keep being filled in for housing and fish farms. West Bengal made it the state animal, instead of the far more famous tiger, partly to draw attention to these fast-disappearing wetlands.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a flagship for the marshes that clean Kolkata's sewage and feed its fish markets.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bengal's state animal is a cat that goes fishing.

sections.title: Before the British: monks, sultans and terracotta
sections.intro_md:
Bengal's soft soil has no good building stone, which shaped its whole history of art. People built in **brick and baked clay**, and wrote on palm leaf, so much has washed away. What survives is still remarkable.

Around the 3rd century BCE, ports in the delta such as **Chandraketugarh** and **Tamralipta** traded with Southeast Asia and Rome. From about **750 CE** the **Pala** kings, Buddhists who ruled from Bengal for four centuries, sponsored huge monasteries and universities and sent teachers to Tibet. The Hindu **Sena** dynasty followed, then in **1204** a Turkic general, Bakhtiyar Khalji, rode into Nadia and Bengal entered more than five centuries of Muslim rule.

The independent **Bengal Sultanate** (1352 to 1576) built mosques with curved roofs that copied village huts, and patronised Bengali poetry. Under the **Mughals**, Bengal became the richest province of the empire, famous for muslin and rice; its last independent rulers, the Nawabs, ruled from **Murshidabad**.

spotlights.name: Adina Mosque, Pandua
spotlights.when: Built 1373 to 1375 by Sultan Sikandar Shah
spotlights.spot_it: A long ruined brick screen of arches, roofless now, with a stone prayer niche and rows of pillars in a grassy courtyard.
spotlights.story_md: When it was finished in **1375**, the Adina Mosque was the **largest mosque in the Indian subcontinent**, built by the second sultan of independent Bengal to announce that his kingdom rivalled Delhi. Hundreds of small brick domes once roofed the cloisters around a vast courtyard. Its builders reused carved stone from older Hindu and Buddhist buildings; you can still spot temple carvings set into the walls, which feeds a modern political argument. Nearby **Gaur**, the sultanate's capital, has brick gateways on the Bangladesh border.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how powerful and independent medieval Bengal was.
spotlights.memory_hook: Once the biggest mosque in India; today a field of arches.

spotlights.name: Terracotta temples of Bishnupur
spotlights.spot_it: A squat brick temple with a curved, hut-like roof, every inch of its walls covered in small red-brown carved tiles.
spotlights.story_md: The Malla kings, Vaishnavas devoted to Krishna, built dozens of temples in a town with no building stone. Their answer was **terracotta**: thousands of baked-clay tiles showing the Ramayana, Krishna's games, hunts, Portuguese ships and soldiers with guns. The **Jor Bangla** temple (1655) joins two village-hut roofs into one. The **Rasmancha** (around 1600) is a stepped pyramid where idols were displayed during festivals. Bishnupur also gave its name to a school of Hindustani music, the **Bishnupur gharana**, and to Baluchari silk weaving.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the finest surviving brick-and-clay temple art in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: Temples that look like village huts, wearing the Ramayana as tiles.

sections.title: How a trading post took over India
sections.intro_md:
The English were latecomers to Bengal. The **Portuguese** settled at Bandel in the 1500s, then came the **Dutch** at Chinsurah, the **Danes** at Serampore and the **French** at Chandannagar, all on the same stretch of the Hooghly. The English East India Company built **Fort William** in Calcutta around 1700.

In **1756** the young Nawab **Siraj ud-Daulah** took Calcutta. A year later, on **23 June 1757**, Robert Clive met him at **Plassey**. The battle was decided before it started: Clive had bribed the Nawab's commander **Mir Jafar**, whose troops stood still. Eight years later the Mughal emperor gave the Company the *diwani*, the right to collect Bengal's taxes. A trading company had become a government.

A famine in **1770** killed millions. Calcutta became capital of British India in 1772 and stayed so until **1911**. Lord Curzon's **partition of Bengal in 1905** set off the Swadeshi movement; it was reversed in 1911, the year the capital moved to Delhi. In **1943** a man-made famine killed about 3 million people. In 1946 riots tore through Calcutta, and in 1947 Bengal was cut in two.

spotlights.name: The Battle of Plassey
spotlights.spot_it: A painting of Clive in a red coat greeting Mir Jafar in a turban, both looking pleased with the deal.
spotlights.story_md: Clive had about **3,000** men; Siraj ud-Daulah had about **50,000**, plus French gunners and war elephants. A downpour soaked the Nawab's gunpowder while the British had covered theirs with tarpaulins. More importantly, Mir Jafar, promised the throne, kept a third of the army out of the fight. The battle lasted a few hours and the Company lost fewer than 25 men. Siraj fled and was killed days later; Mir Jafar became a puppet Nawab. His name became Bengali slang for a traitor. The name Plassey comes from the *palash*, the flame-of-the-forest tree, which once grew thick there.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It began British rule in India and turned a company into an empire.
spotlights.memory_hook: A rainy afternoon, a bribed general, and two centuries of empire.

spotlights.name: Victoria Memorial
spotlights.spot_it: A white marble domed palace in a park of lawns and ponds, a bronze angel turning on top of the dome.
spotlights.story_md: Lord Curzon proposed a memorial to Queen Victoria after her death in 1901, to be paid for by 'voluntary' donations from Indian princes and the public. It is built of white **Makrana marble**, the same as the Taj Mahal, mixing Italian Renaissance and Mughal forms. The bronze **Angel of Victory** on the dome, about 4.9 m tall, was designed to turn with the wind like a weathervane. When the building opened in **1921**, the capital had already moved to Delhi ten years earlier.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the grandest leftover of Calcutta's century as imperial capital.
spotlights.memory_hook: A marble Taj for a queen, finished after the capital had left.

spotlights.name: The Bengal famine of 1943

where.label: Across Bengal, worst in the south

spotlights.spot_it: Black-and-white newspaper photographs of starving people on Calcutta pavements, published by The Statesman in August 1943.
spotlights.story_md: Between **2.1 and 3 million** people died in Bengal in 1943 to 1944, during the Second World War. There was a harvest shortfall and a cyclone, but there was no absolute lack of food. Japan's capture of Burma cut rice imports; war spending and hoarding drove prices up fourfold; the army seized delta boats; and the colonial government was slow to admit a famine at all. Exports were not stopped fast enough, and Churchill's war cabinet turned down or delayed offers of grain shipments, a point historians still argue over. Amartya Sen, who saw it as a boy, later used it to show that famines are about who can afford food, not only supply.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a central example in how economists and historians understand famine.
spotlights.memory_hook: No shortage of rice, and still three million dead.

sections.title: Calcutta's century of ideas
sections.intro_md:
Between about **1815 and 1915**, a small, mostly upper-caste, English-educated Hindu elite in Calcutta argued its way into the modern world. Historians call it the **Bengal Renaissance**. It is overpraised and overcriticised in about equal measure, but its output is not in doubt.

It produced social reformers who fought **sati** and child marriage, educators who wrote the primers every Bengali child still learns from, the first Indian scientists to work at a world level, a monk who took Hindu philosophy to America, and the first Asian Nobel laureate. Institutions came with it: the **Asiatic Society** (1784), **Hindu College** (1817, now Presidency University), the **University of Calcutta** (1857) and the **Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science** (1876), where C. V. Raman did his Nobel-winning work in 1928.

Its limit was real: it largely left out Muslims, the rural poor and lower castes, the majority of Bengal.

spotlights.name: Raja Ram Mohan Roy
spotlights.spot_it: A portrait of a heavily built man in a turban and shawl, painted in Bristol in the 1830s.
spotlights.story_md: Ram Mohan Roy read Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Hebrew, Greek and English, and used them to argue that the Upanishads taught one formless God. His campaign against **sati**, the burning of widows on their husband's pyres, helped persuade Governor-General Bentinck to ban it in **1829**. He founded the **Brahmo Sabha** in 1828, a reformist Hindu movement without idols. The Mughal emperor gave him the title *Raja* and sent him to England as an envoy. He died of meningitis in **Bristol** in 1833 and is buried there, under an Indian-style chhatri at Arnos Vale cemetery.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is often called the father of modern India.
spotlights.memory_hook: The father of modern India is buried in Bristol.

spotlights.name: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
spotlights.spot_it: A stern bald man with a broad face, wearing a plain white chadar and no shirt, often on a statue or a stamp.
spotlights.story_md: Born poor in a village, Vidyasagar ('ocean of learning') is said to have studied under street lamps. He became principal of Sanskrit College and opened it to students of all castes. He campaigned for **widow remarriage**, collected about a thousand signatures and saw the **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act passed in 1856**; he later married his own son to a widow. He also reformed the Bengali alphabet: his primer **Barnaparichay** (1855) cut and reordered the letters, and every Bengali child still learns to read from it or its descendants.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He gave Bengal its modern alphabet and its widows the right to remarry.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who studied under street lamps rewrote the alphabet.

spotlights.name: Swami Vivekananda
spotlights.spot_it: A young monk in a turban and robe, arms folded, staring straight at the camera: the famous 'Chicago pose' photograph.
spotlights.story_md: Narendranath Datta was a Calcutta law student and sceptic who became the disciple of **Ramakrishna**, a mystic priest at Dakshineswar. On **11 September 1893**, at the World's Parliament of Religions in **Chicago**, he opened with 'Sisters and brothers of America' and got a two-minute standing ovation. He then founded the **Ramakrishna Mission** in 1897, combining monastic life with hospitals, schools and disaster relief. He died at **39**. His birthday, 12 January, is India's National Youth Day.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He brought Vedanta to the West and gave Hindu reform a social-service arm.
spotlights.memory_hook: Five words in Chicago, two minutes of applause.

spotlights.name: Jagadish Chandra Bose
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded man in a suit standing beside brass laboratory apparatus with horns and wires.
spotlights.story_md: In **1895**, in a small lab at Presidency College, Bose sent **millimetre-wavelength radio waves** through walls to ring a bell and set off a small charge of gunpowder, two years before Marconi's famous demonstrations. He built some of the first semiconductor detectors but refused to patent most of his work, believing knowledge should be free. Later he turned to plants and built the **crescograph**, which magnified plant growth about 10,000 times, to argue that plants respond to stimuli much like animals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He was among the first Indians to do world-class experimental physics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Radio before Marconi, then he listened to plants.

spotlights.name: Satyendra Nath Bose
spotlights.spot_it: A man with round glasses and a white kurta, sitting with a smile, often shown in his later years.
spotlights.story_md: In **1924**, a 30-year-old lecturer at Dhaka University, Bose wrote a short paper deriving Planck's law of radiation by counting light particles in a new way. British journals turned it down. He mailed it to **Albert Einstein**, who translated it into German himself and had it published. The method became **Bose-Einstein statistics**, and particles that obey it are called **bosons**, after him, including the Higgs boson. Bose never won a Nobel Prize, though several people later won it for work built on his. He was born and died in Calcutta.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Half the particles in the universe are named after a Calcutta physicist.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rejected by journals, rescued by Einstein, remembered in every boson.

sections.title: Bengali, and the poet who wrote two anthems
sections.intro_md:
**Bengali** (Bangla) is one of the most spoken languages on Earth: about **240 million** native speakers in Bangladesh, West Bengal, Tripura and Assam's Barak Valley, roughly the seventh largest by native speakers. In West Bengal **86%** of people gave it as their mother tongue in 2011. On **3 October 2024** India declared it a **classical language**, along with Marathi, Pali, Prakrit and Assamese.

Its script, shared with Assamese, hangs letters from a horizontal headline, like Devanagari, but with rounder shapes. Its oldest surviving texts are the **Charyapada**, Buddhist mystic songs from roughly the 10th to 12th centuries. Bengali's modern literature, from Bankim Chandra's novels to Tagore's songs, made it the first Indian language to win a Nobel Prize.

On **21 February 1952**, students in Dhaka were shot demanding Bengali as a state language of Pakistan; the day is now **International Mother Language Day**.

spotlights.name: Charyapada

where.label: Found in the royal library of Nepal, Kathmandu

spotlights.spot_it: A narrow palm-leaf manuscript page with lines of small, hooked old Bengali letters.
spotlights.story_md: In **1907** the scholar **Haraprasad Shastri**, hunting manuscripts in the Nepal royal library, found a palm-leaf book of **about 50 songs** by Buddhist tantric poets called siddhas. The songs, in a riddling 'twilight language', describe boatmen, hunters, outcaste women and wine sellers as metaphors for the path to enlightenment. Bengali, Assamese, Odia and Maithili scholars all claim the language as the ancestor of theirs, and all have a point. The find pushed Bengali literature back several centuries and showed that its oldest voices were low-caste, rural and Buddhist.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the earliest written evidence of the Bengali language family.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bengali's oldest book was found in Nepal, written in riddles.

spotlights.name: Rabindranath Tagore
spotlights.spot_it: A tall man with a long white beard and flowing robe, usually in profile, looking like a prophet from a painting.
spotlights.story_md: Tagore was the 14th child of a rich Calcutta family and never finished school. He wrote about **2,230 songs**, dozens of plays, novels and thousands of poems, and took up painting in his sixties. In **1913** he became the **first non-European to win a Nobel Prize**, for *Gitanjali*. He wrote the national anthems of **two countries**, India's *Jana Gana Mana* and Bangladesh's *Amar Shonar Bangla*. He returned his British knighthood after the 1919 Jallianwala Bagh massacre. His Nobel medal was **stolen** from Visva-Bharati in 2004 and has never been found. Bengalis call him simply *Kobiguru*, the poet-teacher.
spotlights.why_it_matters: No one has shaped a modern Indian language and culture more.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two countries sing his songs as anthems.

sections.title: Kali, Krishna, the Mission and the forest goddess
sections.intro_md:
In the 2011 census **70.5%** of West Bengal's people were Hindu, **27.0%** Muslim, one of the highest shares of any state, and under 1% Christian, with small Buddhist communities in the hills and Jains in Murshidabad.

Bengali Hinduism leans towards the **goddess**. Durga comes home in autumn; **Kali**, dark, tongue out, garlanded with skulls, is worshipped on the new moon night of Diwali. Bengal is also the home of **Gaudiya Vaishnavism**, the ecstatic devotion to Krishna started by **Chaitanya** (1486 to 1534) of Nabadwip, who danced and sang God's names in the streets. The 'Hare Krishna' movement that spread worldwide in the 1960s is its descendant.

Islam in Bengal spread through Sufi saints who cleared forest and settled the delta, and their shrines, such as **Furfura Sharif** in Hooghly, draw huge crowds. Between and across faiths sit the Bauls, wandering singers, and village deities like **Bonbibi**, the forest goddess both Hindus and Muslims of the Sundarbans pray to before entering tiger country.

spotlights.name: Dakshineswar Kali Temple
spotlights.spot_it: A cream-and-red temple with nine spires stacked in two tiers, on the bank of the Hooghly, with a row of twelve small Shiva shrines.
spotlights.story_md: The temple was built by **Rani Rashmoni**, a rich widow from a lower caste, who is said to have dreamt of Kali. Brahmin priests refused to serve at a temple founded by a woman of her caste, until a poor priest's family agreed. The younger brother, **Ramakrishna**, became the temple priest and went into trances so intense that visitors thought him mad. Among the young men who came to test him was Narendranath Datta, the future Vivekananda.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where the mystic who inspired modern Hindu reform lived and taught.
spotlights.memory_hook: A widow built it, the priests refused it, and a mystic made it famous.

spotlights.name: Belur Math
spotlights.spot_it: A sand-coloured temple by the river whose facade mixes a church window, a mosque dome and a Hindu temple tower.
spotlights.story_md: Belur Math is the headquarters of the **Ramakrishna Math and Mission**, founded by Vivekananda. The main temple, finished in **1938**, was designed to look like a **temple, a mosque and a church** at once, from different angles, to express Ramakrishna's teaching that all religions lead to the same truth. The Mission today runs hospitals, schools, colleges and relief work across India and in more than 20 countries. On Christmas Eve the Math holds a puja to Jesus.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the base of one of India's largest service organisations.
spotlights.memory_hook: One building, three religions, depending on where you stand.

spotlights.name: Bonbibi, lady of the forest
spotlights.spot_it: A small roadside shrine with a painted clay goddess in a crown, often riding a tiger or a chicken, next to a tiger demon figure.
spotlights.story_md: Before going into the Sundarbans for honey or wood, both **Hindus and Muslims** pray to Bonbibi, who protects people from **Dakshin Rai**, a tiger demon. Her story, told in a text called the *Bonbibi Johuranama*, says she came from Mecca, the daughter of a Sufi, and divided the forest so that humans and tigers each keep their part. The tale is performed as village theatre, *Bonbibir pala*. The rules it teaches, take only what you need and never go in greedy, work as a folk conservation code.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She is a living example of shared Hindu-Muslim religion in Bengal.
spotlights.memory_hook: In the mangroves, Hindus and Muslims pray to the same lady before facing the tiger.

sections.title: Songs, masks and the cinema of Satyajit Ray
sections.intro_md:
Bengal's music runs from the Hindustani classical of the Bishnupur gharana to **Rabindra Sangeet**, Tagore's 2,000-plus songs, which Bengalis sing at weddings, funerals, protests and school assemblies. There is **Nazrul Geeti**, the songs of the rebel poet Kazi Nazrul Islam, the national poet of Bangladesh, and the folk traditions of the boatmen (*bhatiali*) and the Bauls.

Theatre has a popular branch, **jatra**, travelling troupes that played all-night melodramas in village fields, and a political branch, the group theatre of the 1940s Indian People's Theatre Association. The **dhak**, a big barrel drum played with two sticks, is the sound of Durga Puja.

And there is cinema. Kolkata's Tollygunge studios (hence 'Tollywood', a nickname older than Bollywood's) made Bengali films from 1919. In the 1950s three directors, **Satyajit Ray, Ritwik Ghatak and Mrinal Sen**, made Bengali cinema famous worldwide. Two Bengal dance and music forms are on UNESCO's intangible heritage list: **Baul songs** (proclaimed 2005) and **Chhau dance** (2010).

spotlights.name: Baul singers

where.label: Kenduli, Birbhum, and across rural Bengal

spotlights.when: Recorded since the 17th to 18th century; UNESCO 2005 (proclaimed), 2008 (inscribed)
spotlights.spot_it: A singer in a saffron patchwork robe and a topknot, plucking a one-string *ektara* while spinning, with a small drum on the hip.
spotlights.story_md: Bauls are wandering mystics, Hindu and Muslim by birth, who reject temples, mosques, caste and scripture. They seek the *moner manush*, 'the person of the heart', the divine within the body. Their most famous poet, **Lalon Fakir** (died 1890), asked in song why people fuss over his caste. Tagore collected Baul songs and was deeply influenced by them. The **ektara** is a gourd with one string, its pitch bent by squeezing two bamboo arms. Each January the **Joydev Kenduli mela** in Birbhum brings thousands of Bauls together. Bob Dylan posed with Baul singers **Purna Das** and Luxman Das on the cover of *John Wesley Harding* (1967).
spotlights.why_it_matters: Their songs are Bengal's sharpest voice against caste and dogma.
spotlights.memory_hook: One string, one robe, no temple: the Baul is the church.

spotlights.name: Purulia Chhau
spotlights.spot_it: Dancers in huge painted papier-mâché masks with towering headdresses of beads and peacock feathers, doing somersaults to drums.
spotlights.story_md: Chhau comes in three styles, from Purulia in Bengal, Seraikela in Jharkhand and Mayurbhanj in Odisha. The **Purulia** style is the most acrobatic and the only one in Bengal: dancers in heavy masks leap, spin and somersault through battles from the Mahabharata and Ramayana, usually Durga against the buffalo demon. The **masks** are made in the village of **Charida**, where dozens of families shape them from clay moulds, paper and cloth; they received a GI tag in 2018. Performances go on through the night after the spring harvest, to the dhol, the *dhamsa* kettle drum and the shehnai.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turns martial training and village myth into a full-body theatre.
spotlights.memory_hook: A mask so big the dancer flips blind.

spotlights.name: Satyajit Ray
spotlights.spot_it: A very tall man (about 1.93 m) with a deep voice, often shown peering through a camera viewfinder or with a pipe.
spotlights.story_md: Ray was a commercial artist at an advertising agency when he saw Vittorio De Sica's *Bicycle Thieves* in London in 1950 and decided to make films. **Pather Panchali** (1955), about a poor village boy named Apu, was shot over three years with amateur actors, money from Ray's life insurance, his wife's jewellery and finally a West Bengal government grant. It won a prize at Cannes in 1956. Ray made **36 films**, wrote detective stories (Feluda) and science fiction (Professor Shonku), designed his own posters and typefaces, and composed his own scores. He received an **honorary Oscar in 1992**, from a hospital bed, weeks before he died.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He put Indian cinema on the world map.
spotlights.memory_hook: A government grant for road building helped pay for Pather Panchali.

sections.title: Running stitch, clay horses and singing scrolls
sections.intro_md:
Bengal's crafts grew from cheap materials and a lot of skill: worn-out saris, river clay, scrap brass, the pith of a marsh weed. Several now carry **Geographical Indication** tags, which protect a name the way Champagne is protected.

The delta was once the world's most famous textile region. Dhaka's **muslin** was so fine that a length could be pulled through a ring; East India Company policy and Lancashire machine cloth helped kill it in the 1800s. What survives on the Indian side includes the cotton **tant** saris of Shantipur, Phulia and Dhaniakhali, the silk of Murshidabad and the picture-woven **Baluchari** of Bishnupur.

The southwest, around Bankura and Bardhaman, is the land of terracotta and metal: long-necked clay horses offered to village gods, and **dokra**, brass cast by the lost-wax method by tribal metalsmiths. In Kolkata's temple lanes and in villages like Naya in Medinipur, painters turned myth and news into pictures for pilgrims and audiences.

spotlights.name: Kantha embroidery
spotlights.spot_it: Soft layered cloth covered in tiny running stitches that ripple the surface, with flowers, fish and figures in coloured thread.
spotlights.story_md: Kantha began as **recycling**: women stacked several old saris and dhotis, quilted them together with a simple **running stitch**, and pulled coloured threads from the old borders to embroider them. The result became baby wraps, quilts and covers for books and mirrors. The densest pieces, *nakshi kantha* or 'patterned quilts', tell stories in pictures, from village weddings to tigers and steamships. Today kantha stitch on silk saris is a major rural industry around Bolpur and Santiniketan, employing tens of thousands of women.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned waste cloth into one of India's best-known embroideries.
spotlights.memory_hook: Old saris, a running stitch, a new story.

spotlights.name: Baluchari sari
spotlights.spot_it: A silk sari whose pallu is a grid of picture panels, each showing a scene from the Mahabharata or Ramayana, in a few colours.
spotlights.story_md: Baluchari began in the village of Baluchar in Murshidabad under the Nawabs, where weavers showed courtly scenes, including men smoking hookahs and riding in horse carriages. When floods destroyed Baluchar and the craft nearly died, it was revived in **Bishnupur** in the mid 1900s by the designer **Subho Thakur** and the master weaver Akshay Kumar Das, using the jacquard loom. Its **pallu** reads like a comic strip. The variety woven with gold thread is called *swarnachari*. It got a **GI tag in 2011**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the few Indian saris that tells a story in pictures.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sari with a comic strip on its tail.

spotlights.name: Bankura horse
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, stylised terracotta horse with a long upright neck, pricked ears and a burnt-red or brown glaze.
spotlights.story_md: The village of **Panchmura** makes the best-known Bankura horses. They are wheel-thrown in parts, the neck and legs as tubes, then joined and fired. Villagers offer them to local deities such as Dharmaraj and Manasa, in thanks for a wish granted, and in some sacred groves you can see hundreds of them standing in rows under trees. The design is so recognisable that the **All India Handicrafts Board** used it as its logo. It is now a stock symbol of Indian folk art, on posters, coasters and hotel lobbies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It became the emblem of Indian handicrafts.
spotlights.memory_hook: A clay horse that lost its body and grew its neck.

spotlights.name: Dokra metal casting
spotlights.spot_it: Small brass figures of elephants, horses, owls and dancers with a rough, rope-textured surface, as if made of coiled thread.
spotlights.story_md: Dokra smiths, traditionally of the **Dhokra Damar** community, use one of the oldest metal techniques known, **lost-wax casting**, the same method as the Harappan 'dancing girl'. A clay core is wrapped in threads of wax, covered in more clay, and heated; the wax runs out and molten brass, often from scrap, is poured in its place. The mould is broken to get the figure out, so **no two pieces are alike**. The 'thread' texture comes from the wax being laid on as fine coils. Bikna in Bankura and Dariyapur in Bardhaman are the main centres in Bengal; Bengal's dokra got a GI tag in 2018.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It keeps alive a casting method used since the Indus Valley.
spotlights.memory_hook: Wax threads in, brass out, mould smashed: every one unique.

spotlights.name: Kalighat painting
spotlights.spot_it: Bold, swelling outlines and flat watercolour on cheap paper: plump goddesses, cats holding fish, dandies and their mistresses.
spotlights.story_md: Painters from rural scroll-painting families moved to the lanes around **Kalighat temple** in the 1800s and sold quick pictures to pilgrims, a sort of souvenir postcard. They worked fast in watercolour on **mill-made paper**, using a few sweeping brushstrokes. Besides gods, they painted the city: babus with oiled hair, women in fashionable shoes, and a famous scandal of 1873, the **Tarakeswar affair**, in which a husband killed his wife after her affair with a temple priest. A **cat with a prawn in its mouth** became a satire on hypocritical holy men. The style later influenced **Jamini Roy**. The best collection is at the V&A in London.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was India's first popular urban art and its first visual satire.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cat holding a prawn: the 19th-century meme for a fake saint.

spotlights.name: Patachitra of Pingla
spotlights.when: Living tradition; Pot Maya festival each November
spotlights.spot_it: A long vertical scroll of painted panels in bright natural colours, unrolled one frame at a time while the painter sings.
spotlights.story_md: In **Naya**, about 250 people of the **patua** community paint long scrolls and sing a song, the *pater gaan*, as they reveal each panel. Many patuas are Muslim by name and practice but paint Hindu epics, Bengal's Mangal Kavya poems and Santal creation stories, a mix centuries old. They have always painted the news too: patuas have made scrolls about the **2004 tsunami**, HIV, Covid-19 and the 9/11 attacks. Colours come from plants and minerals: turmeric, indigo, lamp black, clay. Since 2010 the village has held **Pot Maya**, a yearly festival where visitors can watch and buy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a rare living art where painting and song are one performance.
spotlights.memory_hook: A painter who sings the tsunami frame by frame.

sections.title: Fish, mustard and a sweet tooth
sections.intro_md:
Bengali food is built on **rice and fish**, cooked in **mustard oil**, scented with *panch phoron*, a five-seed mix of fenugreek, nigella, cumin, black mustard and fennel. A proper meal runs in courses, like a French dinner: something bitter first (*shukto*), then dal with fritters, vegetables, fish, perhaps meat, then a sweet-sour chutney, *papor* (papad), and finally sweets and *mishti doi*.

Bengal has some of India's highest rates of fish eating: NFHS data suggest well over 95% of adults eat fish, chicken or meat at least now and then, and even many Brahmins eat fish, calling it 'the fruit of the water'. There are two culinary tribes. **Ghotis**, families native to West Bengal, cook lighter and sweeter; **Bangals**, whose families came from East Bengal, now Bangladesh, especially after 1947, cook hotter and love dried fish. The rivalry carries into football.

Kolkata adds layers: **biryani** from an exiled Nawab, **Chinese** food from Hakka migrants, Jewish bakeries, and street food from phuchka to kathi rolls.

rows.Bangal (East Bengal roots): Dhaka, Barishal or Sylhet accents at home

spotlights.name: Rosogolla
spotlights.when: Modern version usually credited to Nobin Chandra Das, 1868; GI tag 2017
spotlights.spot_it: Spongy, off-white balls of curd cheese floating in thin, clear sugar syrup, squeaky when you bite.
spotlights.story_md: Bengalis credit the spongy rosogolla to **Nobin Chandra Das**, a confectioner of Bagbazar, in **1868**. The trick is *chhena*, fresh cheese made by splitting milk with acid, kneaded smooth and boiled in light syrup. His son K. C. Das began **canning** them in the 1930s, which took rosogolla across India and the world. Odisha says the sweet began centuries earlier as an offering at the **Jagannath temple** in Puri. The fight went to the GI registry: West Bengal got a GI for **Banglar Rosogolla** on **14 November 2017**, and Odisha got its own for **Odisha Rasagola** in **2019**. Both are now protected.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the most famous Bengali sweet and the subject of India's sweetest legal fight.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two states, one sweet, two GI tags.

spotlights.name: Sandesh and nolen gur
spotlights.spot_it: Small pale fudge-like sweets pressed in carved moulds into shells, fish or flowers, sometimes brown with date-palm jaggery.
spotlights.story_md: Sandesh is made from *chhena* kneaded with sugar over gentle heat, then shaped in **wooden or stone moulds**. In winter, Bengalis switch to **nolen gur**, fresh jaggery from date-palm sap, collected by tappers who climb the trees at dusk and come down at dawn with clay pots; it gives a smoky caramel flavour and a brown colour. A famous version, *jolbhora*, has syrup hidden inside and was supposedly invented to trick a son-in-law. **Mishti doi**, sweet yoghurt set in unglazed clay pots that absorb water and thicken it, often comes alongside. Bengali sweet shops are judged by their sandesh more than by their rosogolla.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows Bengal's genius for turning curdled milk into fine art.
spotlights.memory_hook: Winter in Bengal tastes of date-palm smoke.

spotlights.name: Ilish (hilsa)
spotlights.spot_it: A silver, flat, bony fish, often cut into steaks and cooked in a thick yellow paste of ground mustard seed.
spotlights.story_md: Ilish is a sea fish that swims **up rivers to spawn** in the monsoon, and that journey makes it fat and rich. It is famously **bony**, which Bengalis treat as a test of skill. The classic dish is *shorshe ilish*, steamed or simmered in mustard paste and green chillies. Bengalis argue endlessly over whether fish from the **Padma** in Bangladesh beats fish from the Ganga. Bangladesh catches most of the world's ilish and has often banned exports, then sent tonnes to Kolkata as a goodwill **'Puja gift'** before Durga Puja, a practice nicknamed hilsa diplomacy. Overfishing and the Farakka barrage have cut catches on the Indian side.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Bengal's state fish and a currency of diplomacy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bengalis measure skill by how fast you can eat a bony fish.

spotlights.name: Kolkata biryani
spotlights.when: From 1856, after Wajid Ali Shah's exile
spotlights.spot_it: Pale, fragrant, lightly spiced rice with a whole golden potato and a boiled egg sitting next to the meat.
spotlights.story_md: In **1856** the British deposed **Wajid Ali Shah**, the last Nawab of Awadh, and he went into exile at **Metiabruz** in south Kolkata, bringing his cooks, musicians and kite fliers. His cooks adapted the light Awadhi biryani to Bengal. The popular story says they added **potato** because the Nawab's household could no longer afford enough meat; historians point out potatoes were then an exotic luxury, so the addition may have been a delicacy, not a saving. Either way, the **aloo** became the signature, and Bengalis now fight over who gets the potato. The spicing is gentle, with a little nutmeg, mace and rose water.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a dish born of exile, and the potato is non-negotiable.
spotlights.memory_hook: An exiled Nawab, and a potato in the biryani.

spotlights.name: Tiretta Bazaar Chinese breakfast and Tangra
spotlights.spot_it: Folding tables on a street at dawn, selling steamed pork buns, momos, fish ball soup and prawn crackers.
spotlights.story_md: Kolkata had **India's only Chinatown**. The first recorded Chinese settler, **Tong Achew**, set up a sugar mill south of the city around 1778. Hakka families later ran tanneries in **Tangra** and Cantonese families worked as carpenters and dentists. After the **1962** war with China, many were interned in a camp in Rajasthan and thousands left. The community, once perhaps **20,000**, is now a few thousand. Every morning, early, the old Chinatown in **Tiretta Bazaar** holds a street breakfast of buns, dumplings and soups that is gone by about 8 am. Tangra is where **Indian Chinese** food, from chilli chicken to Manchurian, took its modern form.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is where India's favourite cuisine, Indian Chinese, was largely born.
spotlights.memory_hook: Breakfast in Chinatown disappears by eight.

spotlights.name: Darjeeling tea
spotlights.when: Gardens from the 1850s; India's first GI, 2004
spotlights.spot_it: A pale golden cup with a light, flowery, muscatel aroma, from bushes planted on steep terraced slopes.
spotlights.story_md: In **1841** Archibald Campbell, the British superintendent of Darjeeling, planted Chinese tea seeds in his garden as an experiment. Commercial estates followed from the 1850s. Today about **87 gardens** produce Darjeeling tea, under **1% of India's tea** by volume, but at many times the price. The **first flush**, picked in spring, is light and green; the **second flush**, in early summer, has the 'muscatel' grape-like flavour prized in Europe. In **2004** Darjeeling tea became **India's first product with a GI tag**. Output has fallen below 7 million kg a year as yields drop and estates close.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made a Himalayan hill name a luxury brand.
spotlights.memory_hook: Under 1% of India's tea, the first GI in India.

sections.title: Thirteen festivals in twelve months
sections.intro_md:
A Bengali saying goes *baro mashe tero parbon*: **thirteen festivals in twelve months**. Durga Puja dominates the calendar, but it is far from alone.

The Bengali year begins on **Poila Boishakh**, around 14 or 15 April, when shops open fresh red account books, *haal khata*. Spring brings **Dol Jatra**, Bengal's Holi, which at Santiniketan is a festival of songs and yellow clothes. **Rath Yatra** at Mahesh near Serampore claims to be the second oldest chariot festival after Puri's. Autumn is the heavy season: Durga Puja, then **Lakshmi Puja**, then **Kali Puja** on the new moon of Diwali, then **Jagaddhatri Puja** in Chandannagar and Krishnanagar. Winter brings **Poush Sankranti** with rice cakes called *pithe*, the **Gangasagar Mela**, the **Kolkata Book Fair**, Christmas lights on **Park Street**, and Saraswati Puja, when students put their books before the goddess of learning and take the day off.

spotlights.name: Jagaddhatri Puja in Chandannagar
spotlights.when: November, about a month after Durga Puja
spotlights.spot_it: A golden goddess riding a lion over an elephant, surrounded by giant, moving LED light displays that fill whole streets.
spotlights.story_md: Jagaddhatri, 'holder of the world', is a calm, four-armed form of Durga. Her puja was made popular in the 1700s by **Raja Krishnachandra** of Nadia, and its biggest celebration is in **Chandannagar**, a former **French colony** that joined India only after a 1949 referendum. Chandannagar's electricians are famous across India for **light art**: animated displays of trains, dinosaurs or news events built from thousands of bulbs and LEDs. The procession at the end, with giant lit-up trucks, can run all night.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned a small ex-French town into India's capital of festival lighting.
spotlights.memory_hook: A French town in Bengal lights up a goddess with a million bulbs.

spotlights.name: Gangasagar Mela
spotlights.spot_it: Huge crowds of pilgrims wading into grey sea at dawn, with tents, saffron flags and holy men on a flat sandy shore.
spotlights.story_md: Where the Hooghly meets the Bay of Bengal, on **Sagar Island**, pilgrims bathe at **Makar Sankranti** in mid January, at the spot where the Ganga is said to have freed the 60,000 sons of King Sagar. A saying goes *sab tirth bar bar, Gangasagar ek bar*: 'all pilgrimages again and again, Gangasagar just once', from the days when getting there by boat was dangerous. Crowds of several million gather in a few days, which officials often call the biggest **annual** fair in India after the Kumbh years. The **Kapil Muni temple** on the shore has been rebuilt several times as the sea ate the beach.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is one of the largest religious gatherings on Earth, held on a shrinking island.
spotlights.memory_hook: All pilgrimages again and again, Gangasagar once.

sections.title: Adda, books, trams and the derby
sections.intro_md:
Bengalis have a word for the thing they are proudest of doing: **adda**, long, unhurried, argumentative conversation with friends, on a porch, at a tea stall or in a coffee house, about politics, football, films and poetry. Critics call it a waste of time; fans call it Bengal's real university.

The data offer a mixed picture. West Bengal's women have among the **lowest fertility** in India, **1.6** children each (NFHS-5), lower than Sweden's mid-century levels, and the state's **Kanyashree** scheme, which pays girls to stay in school and unmarried, won a UN Public Service Award in 2017. Yet the same survey found **41.6%** of women aged 20 to 24 had married before 18, among the highest in India and unchanged from the previous survey.

City life runs on old machines: yellow **Ambassador taxis** (made until 2014), **hand-pulled rickshaws**, trams from 1873, and a metro that now runs under the Hooghly. And by football: Kolkata's two great clubs, **Mohun Bagan** and **East Bengal**, fill stadiums the way cricket does elsewhere in India.

spotlights.name: Indian Coffee House, College Street
spotlights.spot_it: A high-ceilinged hall of tired tables under slow fans, a giant portrait of Tagore, waiters in white uniforms and turbans.
spotlights.story_md: The Coffee House in the old **Albert Hall** opened in **1942**, run by the Coffee Board, and became Kolkata's most famous adda. Satyajit Ray, the filmmaker Mrinal Sen, the poet Sunil Gangopadhyay, Amartya Sen and generations of student radicals argued here over cheap coffee and mutton cutlets. When the Coffee Board closed it in **1958**, protests forced a reopening, and since then a **workers' cooperative** has run it. A 1983 song by Manna Dey, *Coffee House er sei addata*, lamented the old friends who drifted away, and nearly every Bengali knows it by heart.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the temple of adda and of Bengal's student politics.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cheap coffee, high ceilings, sixty years of arguments.

spotlights.name: Kolkata's trams
spotlights.spot_it: A two-car blue-and-white tram, bell clanging, crawling down the middle of a crowded road under a tangle of overhead wires.
spotlights.story_md: Calcutta's first horse-drawn tram ran in **1873**, and electric trams from **1902**, making it the **oldest electric tram network still running in Asia**. At its peak it had dozens of routes. Trams are slow, and the state government argued they clog roads; routes have been cut year after year. In **2024** the government said most of the network would close, leaving a short heritage stretch, and the Calcutta High Court and citizens' groups pushed back. By 2025 only a couple of routes ran. A tram that ran across the Howrah Bridge stopped in 1993.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a test case for whether Indian cities keep public heritage or clear roads for cars.
spotlights.memory_hook: Asia's oldest electric trams, still clanging, just.

spotlights.name: The Kolkata Derby
spotlights.when: First derby 1921; Mohun Bagan's IFA Shield 1911
spotlights.spot_it: A packed stadium split into green-and-maroon flags on one side and red-and-gold on the other.
spotlights.story_md: On **29 July 1911**, **Mohun Bagan**, most of its players **barefoot**, beat the East Yorkshire Regiment 2 to 1 to win the IFA Shield, the first time an Indian side won the trophy. In **1920** **East Bengal** was founded by families from eastern Bengal after a selection quarrel, and their matches became the **Kolkata Derby**. Mohun Bagan fans are mostly Ghotis and eat prawns; East Bengal fans are Bangals and eat ilish, and on derby day both prices rise. A **1997** derby drew a reported **131,000** people to the Salt Lake Stadium, one of the largest crowds for a club match anywhere.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Asia's oldest great football rivalry and a proxy war between two Bengals.
spotlights.memory_hook: Barefoot in 1911, prawn against hilsa ever since.

sections.title: People to know
sections.intro_md:
Bengal's roll of famous names is long enough to be a cliché, and Bengalis can recite it: **five Nobel laureates** tied to Bengal (Tagore, Amartya Sen, Abhijit Banerjee, Mother Teresa, who made Calcutta her home, and Ronald Ross, who worked out the malaria cycle partly in Calcutta in 1898), plus C. V. Raman, a Tamil whose prize-winning work was done in a Calcutta lab.

Beyond the laureates: freedom fighters from **Subhas Chandra Bose** to the teenage revolutionary **Khudiram Bose**, hanged at 18; singers **Kishore Kumar** and **Manna Dey**; actors **Uttam Kumar** and **Suchitra Sen**; painters **Abanindranath Tagore**, **Nandalal Bose**, who illustrated the original Constitution, and Jamini Roy; scientists from P. C. Ray to Meghnad Saha; cricketers **Sourav Ganguly** and **Jhulan Goswami**; and the economist and politician Jyoti Basu, who ran the state for 23 years.

Here are four whose stories go beyond the textbook line.

spotlights.name: Subhas Chandra Bose (Netaji)
spotlights.spot_it: A stocky man in round glasses and a military cap and uniform, saluting; statues of him stand in nearly every Bengal town.
spotlights.story_md: Born to a Bengali family in Cuttack, Bose passed the elite Indian Civil Service exam in 1920 and resigned to join the freedom struggle. He was twice Congress president but fell out with Gandhi over non-violence and the war. In **January 1941**, under house arrest at his Elgin Road home, he **escaped in disguise as a Pathan insurance agent**, drove to Bihar in a German-made Wanderer car and reached Kabul, then Berlin. He later led the Japanese-backed **Indian National Army**. His death in a plane crash in **Taipei on 18 August 1945** is accepted by most historians, but many Bengalis still dispute it, and three official inquiries have not settled the argument.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is Bengal's most revered political figure and India's great 'what if'.
spotlights.memory_hook: Escaped in disguise, in a Wanderer car, at midnight.

spotlights.name: Mother Teresa

where.label: Mother House, AJC Bose Road, Kolkata

spotlights.spot_it: A small, stooped nun in a white cotton sari with three blue stripes on the border.
spotlights.story_md: Anjezë Gonxhe Bojaxhiu, an ethnic Albanian from Skopje, came to Calcutta in **1929** as a teacher. In 1950 she founded the **Missionaries of Charity**, and her **Nirmal Hriday** home for the dying, next to the Kalighat temple, became world famous. She won the **Nobel Peace Prize in 1979** and asked that the banquet be cancelled and the money given to the poor. She was declared a saint, **Saint Teresa of Calcutta**, on **4 September 2016**. She also drew strong criticism, from Kolkata doctors and from writers such as Christopher Hitchens, for poor medical care in her homes and for her financial dealings.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She made Calcutta's poverty world famous, for better and worse.
spotlights.memory_hook: A sari with three blue stripes, now a trademark.

spotlights.name: Amartya Sen
spotlights.spot_it: A white-haired professor with thick eyebrows and a gentle smile, usually in a kurta or a tweed jacket.
spotlights.story_md: Amartya Sen was born at Santiniketan; **Tagore chose his name**, which means 'immortal'. As a boy of nine he watched people die in the **1943 famine**, and much of his work asks why. He showed that famines often happen without a fall in food supply, because people lose the means to buy it, and argued that **no famine has occurred in a working democracy with a free press**. He won the **Nobel Prize in 1998**. In 2023 Visva-Bharati tried to evict him from part of his family plot, a dispute a court later stayed. A second Bengali economist, **Abhijit Banerjee**, won in 2019.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He changed how the world measures poverty and wellbeing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Named by Tagore, shaped by a famine.

spotlights.name: Sourav Ganguly
spotlights.spot_it: A left-handed batsman in India blue, stepping out of his crease to hit a spinner over long-off.
spotlights.story_md: Ganguly, called **Dada** and the 'Prince of Kolkata', scored a hundred on his Test debut at **Lord's in 1996**. He took over as captain in **2000**, after a match-fixing scandal, and is widely credited with building a fearless young team, including Sehwag, Yuvraj, Harbhajan and Zaheer. At Lord's in **2002**, after India chased 326 to win the NatWest final, he took off his shirt and **waved it from the balcony**, an image every Indian cricket fan knows. He was president of the BCCI from **2019 to 2022**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He is the cricketer who taught Indian teams to stop being polite.
spotlights.memory_hook: A shirt waved at Lord's.

sections.title: Places to go
sections.intro_md:
If you have a week, split it between three Bengals. **Kolkata**: walk the old city from Kumartuli to the Marble Palace, eat in Chinatown at dawn, see the Victoria Memorial and the Indian Museum, and cross the river by ferry at sunset. **The hills**: take the toy train, watch sunrise on Kanchenjunga from Tiger Hill, drink first-flush tea in Darjeeling, and go on to **Kalimpong**, a calmer town of nurseries and monasteries.

The **south and west**: take a boat into the Sundarbans from Godkhali; see Bishnupur's temples and Baluchari looms; walk the red-earth campus of **Santiniketan**, a UNESCO site since 2023; go to **Murshidabad** for the Nawabs' palaces. On the way, stop on the Hooghly at **Serampore** (Danish), **Chandannagar** (French), **Chinsurah** (Dutch) and **Bandel** (Portuguese), five European powers within 40 km.

Best time: **October to March**. Kolkata summers are humid and the monsoon floods the streets; the hills are clearest in October, November and spring.

spotlights.name: Santiniketan
spotlights.spot_it: Classes held under trees on red earth, mud-and-thatch buildings painted with murals, and a glass-walled prayer hall.
spotlights.story_md: Tagore's father bought land here in 1863 for a meditation retreat. In **1901** Rabindranath started a school where **children learned outdoors under trees**, without exams as the centre of life. It became **Visva-Bharati** university in **1921**, meant as a meeting place of world cultures. Artists Nandalal Bose and Ramkinkar Baij made the campus an open-air gallery of murals and sculptures. Satyajit Ray, Indira Gandhi and Amartya Sen studied here. In **September 2023** UNESCO added Santiniketan to the World Heritage List, the first **living university** to be inscribed.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is Tagore's argument about education, built in mud and trees.
spotlights.memory_hook: A school where the classroom is a tree.

spotlights.name: Darjeeling
spotlights.spot_it: A town of colourful houses stacked down a steep ridge, with the toy train in the street and Kanchenjunga floating above clouds.
spotlights.story_md: The British leased Darjeeling from the **Chogyal of Sikkim in 1835** as a sanatorium. It became the summer capital of the Bengal Presidency, with boarding schools, a Gothic church and the Mall. Most people are **Nepali-speaking Gorkhas**, along with Lepchas, Bhutias and Tibetans, and the town has been at the heart of the **Gorkhaland** movement for a separate state, including a violent agitation in the 1980s and a **104-day shutdown in 2017**. Tenzing Norgay, who climbed Everest with Edmund Hillary in 1953, lived here and founded the Himalayan Mountaineering Institute.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the hill town that brands India's best tea and holds its most persistent statehood demand.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leased from a Sikkim king, run on tea, still asking for Gorkhaland.

spotlights.name: Five Europes on the Hooghly
spotlights.spot_it: A white Portuguese church at Bandel, a French strand and promenade at Chandannagar, a Danish Lutheran church at Serampore.
spotlights.story_md: Within about **40 km** of river upstream of Kolkata, you can see traces of **Portugal, the Netherlands, Denmark, France and Britain**. **Bandel Church**, from 1599, is among the oldest Christian churches in Bengal. Chinsurah was **Dutch** until 1825, traded for Sumatra. **Serampore** was Danish, called Frederiksnagore, until 1845; there the Baptist missionary **William Carey** printed Bibles in about 40 languages and founded Serampore College in 1818. **Chandannagar** remained **French** until 1950, and its strand still has a French-style promenade and a museum in the old governor's house.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Bengal was the most fought-over trading coast in Asia.
spotlights.memory_hook: A day trip by river through five European empires.

sections.title: How Bengal earns, and how it lost its lead
sections.intro_md:
In **1947** West Bengal was one of India's most industrial states, with jute mills, engineering, ports and Calcutta's head offices. It then fell behind. Its share of India's industrial output dropped through the 1960s and 1970s, hit by the loss of its jute fields to East Pakistan, freight rules that erased its coal advantage, militant unions and power cuts.

Today its economy, about **₹17 lakh crore** in 2023 to 24, is **India's sixth largest**, but income per person is below the national average. It is India's top producer of **jute** (about three quarters of the national crop) and a top producer of **rice**, vegetables and freshwater fish.

Bengal also exports workers, to Kerala, Gujarat and the Gulf. The decisive moment for its reputation with investors came in **2008**, when Tata Motors pulled its Nano car plant out of **Singur** after farmers' protests.

visual.title: Seats in the assembly: how Bengal's politics flipped

spotlights.name: Jute, the golden fibre

where.label: Hooghly riverside mills and delta farms

spotlights.spot_it: Bundles of long golden fibres drying on bamboo poles, or rows of chimneys of brick mills along the Hooghly.
spotlights.story_md: Jute is a tall plant whose stalks are soaked (*retted*) in ponds for weeks until the fibre can be stripped. The first jute mill opened at **Rishra** on the Hooghly in **1855**, using Scottish machinery and know-how from **Dundee**. By 1900 Calcutta had overtaken Dundee as the **jute capital of the world**, making the sacks that carried the world's grain, sugar and cotton. India still requires that much of its foodgrain be packed in jute, which keeps about **70 mills** and around 4 million farm families going.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It built Calcutta's industrial fortune and still feeds millions of farmers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Calcutta beat Dundee at its own sack.

spotlights.name: Singur and Nandigram
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny, rounded, egg-shaped car, the Tata Nano, launched in 2008 as the 'one lakh car'.
spotlights.story_md: In **2006** the Left Front government acquired about **997 acres** of farmland at Singur for Tata Motors to build the **Nano**, the 'people's car' meant to cost ₹1 lakh. Farmers who did not want to sell protested, led by **Mamata Banerjee**, who went on a **26-day hunger strike**. In **Nandigram**, police firing on villagers resisting a chemical hub killed **14 people** on **14 March 2007**. In **October 2008** Ratan Tata pulled the Nano plant out of Bengal and moved it to **Sanand, Gujarat**. The anger ended the Left's 34-year rule in 2011. In 2016 the Supreme Court ordered the land returned.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It ended the world's longest-serving elected communist government and still shapes investor views of Bengal.
spotlights.memory_hook: A car for one lakh rupees cost a government its 34-year reign.

sections.title: What is happening now (2024 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
West Bengal politics has had three long eras. **Congress** ruled from 1947 to 1967, then came years of unstable coalitions. The **Left Front**, led by the CPI(M), ruled for **34 years, 1977 to 2011**, the longest democratically elected communist government in the world. Its land reform, **Operation Barga**, protected sharecroppers; its record on industry was poor. **Mamata Banerjee**'s Trinamool Congress ruled for **15 years, 2011 to 2026**, with cash schemes for women such as **Lakshmir Bhandar**.

The last two years were turbulent. In **August 2024** the rape and murder of a trainee doctor at **R. G. Kar Medical College** set off months of protests; a civic volunteer got life in prison in **January 2025**. In **April 2025** the Supreme Court cancelled about **25,000** school jobs filled through a corrupt 2016 recruitment. In **September 2025**, **251 mm** of rain in a day, the most since 1986, killed at least 10 people in Kolkata days before Durga Puja.

Then came the **2026 assembly election**, held on **23 and 29 April**. A revision of voter rolls had removed around **9 million** names, which the opposition called targeted. Turnout was a record **93.7%**. On **4 May 2026** the **BJP won 208 of 294 seats**, its first ever victory in Bengal; Trinamool fell to 80. Mamata Banerjee lost her own seat, Bhabanipur.

spotlights.name: Mamata Banerjee
spotlights.spot_it: A small woman in a plain white cotton sari with a thin border, rubber slippers and a shoulder bag, walking fast at the head of a rally.
spotlights.story_md: Mamata Banerjee grew up in a lower-middle-class family in Kalighat and rose as a Congress street fighter. In **1990** she was nearly killed when a CPI(M) activist hit her on the head during a protest. She founded the **Trinamool ('grassroots') Congress** in **1998**, served twice as Railway Minister, and used Singur and Nandigram to defeat the Left in **2011**, becoming the state's first woman chief minister. Her schemes, from bicycles for schoolgirls to monthly cash for women, were popular; her government was dogged by charges of corruption and political violence. In **2026**, after 15 years, she lost power and her own seat.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She ended 34 years of Left rule and dominated Bengal for 15 years.
spotlights.memory_hook: White sari, rubber chappals, 15 years in power.

spotlights.name: Suvendu Adhikari
spotlights.spot_it: A man with a neat beard and a saffron or white kurta, a gamchha around his neck, at the front of a BJP rally.
spotlights.story_md: Suvendu Adhikari was once Mamata Banerjee's lieutenant: he led the **Nandigram** movement in **2007** that helped bring her to power, and served in her cabinet. In **December 2020** he defected to the BJP, and in **2021** he beat Banerjee in Nandigram by **1,956 votes**. In **2026** he contested both Nandigram and her home seat, **Bhabanipur**, won both, and kept Bhabanipur. He was sworn in as **West Bengal's first BJP chief minister** on **9 May 2026** at the Brigade Parade Ground in Kolkata. His government's first months brought Ayushman Bharat health insurance to the state and a budget in **June 2026** that proposed five new districts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He leads the first BJP government in a state the party had never won.
spotlights.memory_hook: Mamata's former lieutenant beat her twice, then took her chair.

sections.title: Myths and facts
sections.intro_md:
**Myth: Job Charnock founded Calcutta on 24 August 1690.** Charnock did land there and set up a Company post, but people had lived in the villages for centuries. In **2003** the Calcutta High Court ruled that the city has no founder and no birthday, after a petition by a family that held the villages' revenue rights.

**Myth: 146 British prisoners were locked in the 'Black Hole of Calcutta' in 1756 and 123 died.** The numbers come from one survivor, **John Zephaniah Holwell**, who had reasons to exaggerate. Historians accept that prisoners died in a small cell, but many think the toll was far smaller, perhaps a few dozen.

**Myth: Tagore wrote Sri Lanka's national anthem.** Its author was **Ananda Samarakoon**, who studied under Tagore at Santiniketan. Some claim Tagore wrote the tune or Bengali original; most scholars reject this. Tagore's two anthems are India's and Bangladesh's.

**Myth: 'City of Joy' is an old Bengali nickname.** It comes from **Dominique Lapierre's 1985 novel** about a Calcutta slum.

**Fact, though it sounds like myth: the Howrah Bridge has no nuts and bolts.** It is riveted throughout.

sections.title: Recap: West Bengal in ten lines
sections.intro_md:
1. The only state that runs from the **Himalaya to the sea**.
2. **91 million** people in 2011; density second only to Bihar.
3. Company rule began at **Plassey, 1757**; Calcutta was capital until **1911**.
4. The **Bengal Renaissance**: Ram Mohan Roy, Vidyasagar, Vivekananda, the Boses, **Tagore**.
5. **Bengali**: a classical language since **2024**.
6. UNESCO lists: **Durga Puja** (2021), **Chhau**, **Baul songs**, the **toy train**, the **Sundarbans**, **Santiniketan**.
7. Crafts: **kantha, Baluchari, Bankura horse, dokra, Kalighat painting, patachitra**.
8. Food: **rice, fish, mustard**, rosogolla, potato biryani, Darjeeling tea.
9. Politics: Left **1977 to 2011**, Trinamool **2011 to 2026**, BJP since **May 2026**.
10. Kolkata keeps the past running: trams, rickshaws, and a metro under the river.

best_facts.fact: The Howrah Bridge has no pillars in the river and no nuts and bolts; it is riveted throughout, and chewed tobacco spit corroded its steel so badly that the pillar hoods had to be armoured.
best_facts.why_surprising: A war-time engineering icon threatened mainly by spit.

best_facts.fact: Satyendra Nath Bose's paper was rejected by British journals; he mailed it to Einstein, who translated it himself, and today every boson, including the Higgs, carries Bose's name.
best_facts.why_surprising: Half the particles in the universe are named after a Calcutta lecturer.

best_facts.fact: Tagore wrote the national anthems of two countries, India and Bangladesh, and his Nobel medal was stolen from Visva-Bharati in 2004 and never found.
best_facts.why_surprising: One poet, two anthems, one missing medal.

best_facts.fact: Sundarbans forest officers once gave villagers face masks to wear on the back of their heads, because tigers usually attack from behind.
best_facts.why_surprising: A conservation tool that looks like a joke but worked for a while.

best_facts.fact: In 2026 the BJP won West Bengal for the first time, with 208 of 294 seats, on a record 93.7% turnout, and Mamata Banerjee lost her own seat.
best_facts.why_surprising: A state the BJP had never ruled flipped in one election.

best_facts.fact: At the Battle of Plassey in 1757, about 3,000 Company troops beat an army of about 50,000, because the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar had been bribed to stand still.
best_facts.why_surprising: An empire won by a bribe on a rainy afternoon.

best_facts.fact: The Calcutta High Court ruled in 2003 that Job Charnock did not found Calcutta and that the city has no official birthday.
best_facts.why_surprising: A court abolished a city's birthday.

best_facts.fact: Kolkata biryani's famous potato is usually blamed on poverty in an exiled Nawab's kitchen, but potatoes were an exotic luxury in 1850s Bengal.
best_facts.why_surprising: The cheap filler story may be backwards.

best_facts.fact: Ram Mohan Roy, often called the father of modern India, is buried in Bristol, England, under an Indian-style chhatri.
best_facts.why_surprising: A founder of modern India lies in an English cemetery.

best_facts.fact: Bob Dylan's 1967 album John Wesley Harding has two Bengali Baul singers, Purna Das and Luxman Das, on its cover.
best_facts.why_surprising: Bengal's mystic minstrels on a rock album sleeve.

best_facts.fact: West Bengal and Odisha fought over who invented the rosogolla, and both won: Bengal got a GI tag in 2017, Odisha in 2019.
best_facts.why_surprising: India's sweetest legal dispute ended in a draw.

best_facts.fact: Jagadish Chandra Bose sent millimetre radio waves through walls in Calcutta in 1895, before Marconi's famous demonstrations, and refused to patent most of his work.
best_facts.why_surprising: A wireless pioneer who chose not to profit.

best_facts.fact: Mohun Bagan won the 1911 IFA Shield against a British army team with most of its players barefoot.
best_facts.why_surprising: A football match that felt like a freedom fight.

best_facts.fact: From Sandakphu, West Bengal's highest point, you can see four of the world's five highest mountains, including Everest.
best_facts.why_surprising: A sea-level state with a view of Everest.

best_facts.fact: Belur Math's main temple was designed to look like a Hindu temple, a mosque and a church at once, depending on where you stand.
best_facts.why_surprising: Architecture as an argument for religious unity.

best_facts.fact: West Bengal's state animal is not the tiger but the fishing cat, which scoops fish out of water with its paw.
best_facts.why_surprising: The tiger state chose a wetland cat.

best_facts.fact: NFHS-5 found West Bengal women have just 1.6 children each, yet 41.6% of women aged 20 to 24 married before 18, among the highest rates in India.
best_facts.why_surprising: Low fertility and high child marriage in the same state.

side_dish.title: Why mangroves breathe through their feet
side_dish.body_md:
The Sundarbans grows in mud that is flooded by salt water twice a day. That mud has almost no oxygen: water fills every gap between the particles, and bacteria use up what little oxygen gets in. Roots, like every living cell, need oxygen to burn sugar for energy.

Mangroves solve this with **pneumatophores**, roots that grow upward out of the mud like pencils or snorkels. Their bark is dotted with small pores called **lenticels**, which let air in at low tide. Inside, the root is full of spongy tissue, called aerenchyma, with air channels that carry oxygen down to the buried roots. When the tide covers them, the pressure inside drops as the trapped oxygen is used, and when the tide falls, air is pulled back in.

Salt is the other problem. Some mangroves block most salt at the root surface with a kind of ultra-fine filter. Others let salt in and push it out through **salt glands** on their leaves; on a dry day you can see white crystals on them. Some species dump salt into old leaves that they then drop.

The result is a forest that does a job no wall can do as cheaply. Studies of cyclones in Bengal and Odisha found that mangrove belts reduce storm surges and wind damage behind them, and the Sundarbans stores large amounts of carbon in its mud. Next time you see the spiky floor of a mangrove at low tide, you are looking at a forest breathing.

offline_task.title: Make a simple Bengali posto or mustard dish
offline_task.body_md:
Bengali cooking turns on two seeds: **mustard** and **poppy (posto)**. Try one tonight.

**Aloo posto (serves 2):** soak 3 tablespoons of white poppy seeds in warm water for 20 minutes, then grind to a paste with 1 or 2 green chillies. Heat 2 tablespoons of mustard oil until it just smokes, then lower the heat. Add half a teaspoon of nigella seeds (kalonji) and 2 slit green chillies. Add 2 potatoes cut into small cubes, a pinch of turmeric and salt, and fry for 5 minutes. Add the poppy paste and half a cup of water, cover, and cook until the potatoes are soft and the paste clings to them. Finish with a teaspoon of raw mustard oil on top.

Eat it with plain rice and dal, Bengali style: rice first, a little dal poured over, the posto on the side. If you eat fish, try the same mustard oil with a quick mustard-seed paste over a fish steak instead.

While you eat, notice the sharp heat of raw mustard oil, which no other Indian cuisine uses so boldly.
